name: Nume
confidence_why: François 2005, the only work that mentions stress at all, gives a penultimate-stress generalization for the protoforms of all seventeen northern Vanuatu languages in a historical vowel study without describing Nume itself, and Tryon 1976's unmarked wordlist and the rest of the Nume bibliography (Codrington 1885, Lynch & Crowley 2001, François 2011) say nothing, so no stress rule can be stated for Nume and no source disagrees with that.

catalog_quote: In a protoform with two syllables, only the one receiving stress was preserved, while the unstressed vowel eventually disappeared (e.g., *mate > mat). ... this resulted in vowel-final lexemes that systematically received primary stress on their penultimate syllable, and secondary stress every second syllable leftward (e.g., *saŋapulu). Vowel reduction affected word-medial as well as word-final posttonic syllables, which explains why words with four syllables were regularly reduced to two: for example, *saŋapulu > MSN saŋwul. The loss of word-final posttonic vowels explains why, in essentially all the languages of the area, words are now systematically stressed on their final rather than their penultimate syllable (contra Lynch 2000:77). (2) Deciding source: a 2005 comparative-historical vowel study whose only stress sentence is a hedged areal/diachronic generalization over 17 languages; Nume is in the sample and grouped with the final-vowel-losing Mwesen-type languages, but is never individually described as final-stressed, so not determinable is the faithful reading (sibling records on the same sentence were coded the same way; Lakon was upgraded only because François's Pangloss Lakon page says 'Stress is word-final', and the parallel Nume page, held, has no such line).
